architecture.mechanism: Persistence of electricity consumption habits causes inertia and inefficient energy usage.
architecture.intervention: Implement a smart adaptive controller in the refrigerator that learns door-opening and loading habits, then preemptively adjusts cooling cycles to minimize energy waste from habitual over-cooling.
architecture.expected_effect: Reduced energy consumption while maintaining required cooling capacity.
architecture.falsification_test: Run two identical fridges with same load and usage pattern, one with adaptive controller and one without; measure energy over a week; if adaptive does not show >10% reduction, mechanism fails.

architecture.mechanism: food items have composition-dependent metabolic decay rates; cooling that is matched to each item's actual biochemical state (not to user habits) minimizes energy waste while maximizing preservation
architecture.intervention: embed a low-cost NIR/Raman spectroscopic sensor in each refrigerator compartment that continuously estimates the fat/protein/carbohydrate composition and ripeness state of stored items; a controller adjusts compartment temperature and humidity setpoints per-item-group to the minimum cooling that keeps each composition class's metabolic decay below a threshold
architecture.expected_effect: 20-35% reduction in cooling energy versus habit-based control, with equal or better preservation quality (measured by vitamin retention and microbial load)
architecture.falsification_test: place two identical refrigerators with identical food loads (one habit-based, one compositional-state-based) for 14 days; if the compositional controller does not reduce energy by at least 15% at equal preservation quality, the mechanism is falsified

preserved_objections.basis: The mechanism assumes food metabolic heat dominates cooling load, but refrigerator energy is dominated by heat infiltration and door openings; metabolic heat of food is negligible (<1% of load), so adjusting to composition cannot yield 20-35% savings.

The mechanism requires per-item-group temperature/humidity control, but standard refrigerators have a single evaporator and no ability to set different conditions for different items; no boundary conditions are claimed, making the claim unbounded and unrealistic.

The cited evidence (EuropePMC on milk blending for cheese) is irrelevant to refrigerator energy or spectroscopy; it does not support the mechanism, and the arxiv records are about thermodynamic cycles, not food preservation.

The baseline habit-based control already optimizes for usage; the compositional controller would either raise temperature (degrading preservation) or not change energy, so it cannot beat baseline at equal preservation quality; the claimed 15% reduction is unsupported.

Embedding NIR/Raman sensors in each compartment is impractical: Raman signals are weak, sensors cannot see through packaging or cluttered items, and per-item tracking is impossible; multiple compartments with independent control would require major hardware redesign and cost.

The testable prediction lacks defined metrics for "equal preservation quality" (vitamin retention and microbial load are not specified thresholds) and does not control for sensor accuracy or food load variability; a 14-day test is insufficient to establish long-term equivalence.
